column2: In Git, what do blobs, trees and commits represent?
column3: Blobs store file content; trees map names to blobs or subtrees; commits identify a root tree, parents and commit metadata.

column2: What does Git HEAD usually reference, and what is detached HEAD?
column3: Usually the current branch reference; detached HEAD points directly to a commit instead.

column2: How does a Git branch differ from a lightweight tag?
column3: A branch reference advances with new commits; a lightweight tag ordinarily stays attached to a chosen object.

column2: Can two Git branch names identify the same commit?
column3: Yes. Branch names are references; distinct references can point to the same commit.

column2: Which Git operation applies a selected existing commit's changes onto the current branch?
column3: git cherry-pick; it normally creates a new commit with a new identity.

column2: Which Git operation undoes a published commit without removing it from shared history?
column3: git revert, which creates a new commit reversing the selected change.

column2: How does Git reset differ from revert?
column3: Reset moves the current branch tip and may change the index or working tree, depending on mode; revert records an inverse change.

column2: When would you choose rebase instead of merge for a private feature branch?
column3: To replay its commits on an updated base for linear history, accepting that replayed commits acquire new identities.

column2: When is a fast-forward merge possible in Git?
column3: When the current branch tip is an ancestor of the incoming tip; the reference can advance without a new merge commit.

column2: What integration is needed when two Git branch tips have diverged and you choose merge?
column3: A three-way merge using their common ancestor, normally producing a commit with both branch tips as parents.

column2: What should follow editing conflict markers during a Git merge?
column3: Check the intended combined behaviour, stage the resolved files and complete the merge; do not blindly choose one side.

column2: What does a valid commit signature establish, and what does it not establish?
column3: Integrity and association with the signing key under the verifier's trust model; it does not prove code quality or freedom from malware.

column2: Why cannot local Git hooks alone enforce repository policy?
column3: Users can bypass or modify them, and hooks are not automatically installed by cloning; enforce critical rules on the server.

column2: How does trunk-based development keep mainline releasable?
column3: Integrate small changes frequently, run fast automated checks, and fix or revert failures promptly; hide incomplete functionality when needed.

column2: In the original GitFlow model, where do feature branches start and finish?
column3: They branch from develop and merge back into develop.

column2: In GitFlow, where must a production hotfix normally be integrated?
column3: Into the production branch and the development line; if a release branch exists, integrate there as the model requires.

column2: What is the normal lifecycle of a feature branch?
column3: Branch from the intended base, make focused changes, validate and review, integrate, then remove the obsolete branch.

column2: When does a hotfix branch make more sense than a new release branch?
column3: When repairing an already released version urgently while unrelated upcoming work must stay out of production.

column2: Why do long-lived branches increase integration risk?
column3: They accumulate divergent changes, delaying feedback and making conflicts and incompatible assumptions harder to resolve.

column2: How can a feature flag reduce the need for a long-lived feature branch?
column3: Integrate code early while keeping its user-visible behaviour disabled until ready.
